title: The Delivery Locker That Moved the Traffic Problem
passage:
An apartment district struggled with delivery traffic. Online shopping had increased the number of vans entering narrow residential streets, and drivers sometimes stopped briefly in places that blocked bicycles or waste collection. Residents complained about congestion, while delivery companies said repeated failed deliveries forced drivers to return multiple times. The district proposed shared parcel lockers near the main entrance so packages could be delivered without every van visiting every building.

The first lockers were popular with some residents, especially people who worked during the day. Delivery companies liked the ability to leave several packages in one stop. Traffic counts showed fewer vans entering the deepest residential streets. From one perspective, the project was clearly working. Yet the entrance area around the lockers became busier. Vans now concentrated there, and residents collecting packages sometimes arrived by car on their way home.

The district had reduced traffic in one place while increasing activity in another. Planners mapped the new pattern. The entrance was near a bicycle route and a bus stop, so poorly parked delivery vans could still create hazards. The original design had treated the locker as an object to install, not as a small logistics hub requiring space for loading, walking, cycling, and queuing.

The site was redesigned. Two short loading bays were marked for delivery vehicles, with time limits during the busiest hours. A protected bicycle path was moved behind the waiting area rather than through it. Lighting was improved for evening users, and the locker screens were angled to reduce glare. These changes used more land than the original locker bank, but they acknowledged the activities that the system generated.

Another problem involved package size. Standard lockers handled most parcels but not groceries needing refrigeration or very large items. If residents assumed the lockers would eliminate home delivery entirely, they were disappointed. The district added a small refrigerated section, but large items continued to go directly to buildings. Clear communication reduced confusion about which deliveries could use the system.

Equity concerns also appeared. Some older residents found the touchscreen difficult, and people without smartphones could not use the original digital code easily. A physical card option and larger-text interface were added. Building staff were trained to help, but planners avoided making assistance dependent on a single employee being present. Accessibility had to be built into the system rather than offered only as an exception.

Delivery companies supplied data showing fewer failed deliveries and shorter total driving distance within the district. However, researchers cautioned that some of the saved distance might reappear elsewhere if drivers changed routes or if residents made separate trips to collect packages. Surveys showed most residents combined collection with walking home or another trip, while a minority drove specifically to the locker. The environmental benefit therefore depended partly on user behavior beyond the delivery vehicle itself.

The district considered adding more locker sites. Instead of placing one at every building, it chose locations near routes people already used: the transit stop, a small supermarket, and the community center. The goal was to make collection part of existing movement rather than create new journeys.

After two years, delivery vans still entered the neighborhood. The project had not ‘solved’ delivery traffic. It had changed its pattern. The deepest streets were quieter, failed deliveries decreased, and residents gained flexibility, but the main entrance required better design and management.

The experience illustrated a principle common in infrastructure planning: a solution can move a problem rather than remove it. Concentrating deliveries made the system more efficient, but concentration itself created a busy point. The correct question was not whether lockers reduced van numbers in isolation. It was whether the entire chain—from sorting and driving to loading, collection, and final movement—worked better for the neighborhood. Once planners followed that chain, the locker stopped being a box on the sidewalk and became part of a larger transport system.
translation:
集合住宅地区ではネット通販の増加で配送車が細い住宅道路へ入り、短時間の停車が自転車やごみ収集を妨げる問題がありました。再配達も多いため、地区入口に共同宅配ロッカーを置き、各建物まで車が入らなくて済む仕組みを試しました。

深い住宅道路へ入る車は減り、再配達も減りましたが、今度は入口周辺に配送車と荷物を取りに来る住民が集中しました。問題を消したのではなく、場所を移した面がありました。

入口は自転車道とバス停に近く、停車車両が危険になるため、ロッカーを単なる箱ではなく、小さな物流拠点として考え直しました。短時間積み下ろし区画を作り、自転車道を待機場所の後ろへ移し、照明や画面の見やすさも改善しました。

標準ロッカーには冷蔵品や大型荷物が入らないため、小さな冷蔵区画を追加しましたが、大型品は従来通り建物へ配送しました。『すべての宅配がロッカーになる』わけではないことも明確に説明しました。

高齢者にはタッチ画面が使いにくく、スマートフォンがない人もいたため、物理カードと大きな文字の画面を追加しました。特定職員の手助けだけに頼らず、最初から使いやすさを組み込む必要がありました。

配送会社のデータでは、地区内の走行距離と再配達は減りました。ただし住民が荷物だけを取りに車で来れば、別の移動が増えます。調査では多くの人が帰宅や買い物と組み合わせて受け取っていましたが、一部は専用の車移動をしていました。

追加ロッカーは各建物ではなく、バス停、スーパー、地域センターなど人が元々通る場所に置きました。受け取りのための新しい移動を作らないためです。

二年後も配送車は地区から消えていません。しかし奥の道路は静かになり、再配達は減り、受取の自由度も上がりました。一方、入口の管理は必要になりました。

この経験は、インフラ対策が問題を『消す』のではなく『移す』ことがあると示します。ロッカーの評価は配送車台数だけでなく、仕分け、走行、停車、受取、最後の移動まで全体として良くなったかで判断する必要があります。
